title: Phenolic Composition and Antioxidant Capacity of High-Mountain Wild Blueberries
metaDescription: A study analyzes the phenolic composition and antioxidant capacity of wild blueberries compared with high-mountain blackberries in Türkiye.
excerpt: Researchers evaluated in the lab the phenolic composition and antioxidant capacity of high-mountain wild blueberries, identifying chlorogenic acid as their main compound.
imageAlt: Fresh high-mountain blueberries with their natural bloom on a wooden surface

blocks.text: Introduction: the value of wild high-mountain fruits

Wild fruits that grow in high-mountain areas have drawn great interest in food science. The environmental conditions at high altitude, where plants are exposed to temperature swings and particular levels of radiation, tend to directly influence the development of their secondary metabolites. Among these compounds, phenols and flavonoids stand out, plant substances recognized for their physicochemical properties.

Understanding the chemical makeup of these species not only helps appreciate the native biodiversity of different geographic regions, but also shows how their nutritional profiles vary compared with other fruits of the same genus. A recent analysis addressed precisely the characterization of wild blueberry and blackberry populations in mountainous terrain, providing concrete data on their phenolic content and behavior in lab tests.
What the source says: the findings of the lab analysis

The research, published in the journal Molecules, used in vitro assays to evaluate the phenolic profiles and antioxidant capacities of fresh wild fruits collected in the high-mountain region of Akılbaba (Giresun), in the Eastern Black Sea area of Türkiye. The analysis compared samples of wild blackberry (Rubus spp., n = 5) and wild blueberry (Vaccinium spp., n = 4).

To carry out the evaluation, the researchers prepared methanolic extracts of the fresh fruits and determined total phenolic content (TPC), total flavonoid content (TFC) and antioxidant activity using two lab methods: ferric reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) and the DPPH radical scavenging assay. They also identified and quantified individual phenolic compounds using high-performance liquid chromatography (RP-HPLC-PDA) against 25 standards.

The results showed average TPC values of 5.86 ± 1.25 mg GAE/g fresh weight for the wild blueberry and 4.49 ± 0.29 mg GAE/g for the wild blackberry. As for flavonoid content (TFC), the blueberry recorded 0.47 ± 0.13 mg QE/g fresh weight, compared with 0.06 ± 0.03 mg QE/g in the blackberry.

In the FRAP assay, the reducing capacity values were very similar between the two fruits: 95.30 ± 13.26 µmol FeSO4·7H2O E/g for the blueberry and 96.08 ± 9.92 µmol FeSO4·7H2O E/g for the blackberry. However, in the DPPH test, the blackberry showed significantly higher radical-scavenging activity.

The chromatographic analysis showed that chlorogenic acid was the main phenolic constituent in the wild blueberry, while ellagic and gallic acids predominated in the blackberry. The flavonoids chrysin and pinocembrin were detected as common markers in all the samples analyzed.

As a limitation of the study, the authors note that this is an in vitro characterization based on lab extracts with a limited sample size (n = 4 for blueberries and n = 5 for blackberries), so its results are limited to direct chemical measurement and do not evaluate effects in living organisms or human metabolic processes.
Context: how this study compares with existing knowledge

The finding that chlorogenic acid is the dominant phenolic compound in wild blueberries is consistent with previous scientific literature on the Vaccinium genus. This phenolic acid is widely studied in food chemistry because it is present in many commonly eaten fruits and plants.

The study also confirms that measuring antioxidant capacity depends largely on the method used in the lab. While the FRAP technique showed an equivalent potential between the two fruits, the DPPH method showed marked differences because of the specific chemical mechanisms of each assay. This reinforces the idea that the bioactive profiles of fruits are complex and multifaceted.
What it means for you: implications for your daily diet

For consumers, this kind of study offers a clear view of the nutritional richness of small fruits. Knowing that blueberries contain compounds such as chlorogenic acid and various flavonoids helps you value including them in a balanced diet in a conscious, well-informed way.

Adding fresh blueberries to your daily routine, whether at breakfast with oats, in salads or as a snack between meals, is a practical way to enjoy plant-based foods with a varied matrix of phytonutrients, without relying on exaggerated claims or processed supplements.

The characterization of high-mountain wild blueberries shows that these fruits hold well-defined phenolic profiles, notable for the presence of chlorogenic acid and a significant concentration of flavonoids in lab tests.
